title: Scrum, Kanban, Lean and Lean Startup
blurb: Recognize the popular agile approaches from their defining features, and see how PRINCE2 Agile works alongside them.
question: A support team handles a continual stream of requests of different sizes, has no fixed iteration cadence and wants to expose bottlenecks. Which popular agile approach fits best, and what is its defining feature?

teach.body: Agile is a family of approaches rather than one method. The PRINCE2 Agile syllabus asks you to recall four popular ones: Scrum, Kanban, Lean and Lean Startup. You may also meet eXtreme Programming (XP), known for engineering practices such as test-first programming. PRINCE2 Agile does not replace any of them: it adds project direction and management around whichever delivery approach the teams use.

rows.label: Cadence
values: Sprint of a month or less

teach.body: The PRINCE2 Agile glossary calls Scrum an iterative, timeboxed approach to product delivery: in the Scrum Guide's words, a lightweight framework that helps people, teams and organizations generate value through adaptive solutions for complex problems. Work happens in sprints of one month or less. Scrum names three accountabilities: product owner, Scrum master and developers. PRINCE2 Agile uses 'iteration' as its general word for a sprint.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 Glossary; The Scrum Guide (November 2020)

teach.body: Kanban improves flow and provokes system improvement by visualizing work and controlling work in progress (WIP). It is a pull system: new work is pulled in only when there is capacity, and limiting the number of items in circulation exposes bottlenecks. Kanban does not require sprints or fixed iterations, so it suits a continual stream of varied work.

teach.h: A Kanban board: work is pulled
teach.caption: When 'Review' is full, nothing more moves in: the queue in front of it shows the bottleneck.

teach.body: Lean focuses on delivering value with less waste: understand what the customer values, then remove anything that does not add to it and keep improving the flow of work. Lean Startup was originally an approach to creating and managing start-up companies but is now applied to any business to deliver products to customers quickly. Its engine is build-measure-learn: build a minimum viable product, measure the response, learn, then pivot or persevere.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 Glossary; lean.org; theleanstartup.com

teach.body: At Saltmarsh Logistics, the warehouse IT team handles support tickets on a Kanban board with WIP limits. A product team builds a new route-planning app in two-week Scrum sprints. An innovation unit tests a same-day delivery idea with a Lean Startup MVP in one town. Project manager Ines Carvalho runs the route-planning work as a PRINCE2 Agile project, governing it without dictating how the team runs its sprints.

teach.text: Kanban is defined by flow and WIP limits, not by sprints; Scrum is the sprint-based one. Lean is about removing waste, while Lean Startup is the build-measure-learn approach that began with start-ups. XP is known for test-first engineering, not for sprints as its core structure.

items: Scrum: iterative, timeboxed product delivery in sprints of one month or less.
Kanban: visualize work, limit WIP, pull work in; iterations optional.
Lean: maximize value by removing waste. Lean Startup: build-measure-learn, MVP, pivot or persevere.
PRINCE2 Agile adds direction and management around whichever approach the teams use.

summary: You can now recognize Scrum, Kanban, Lean and Lean Startup from their defining features and tell the commonly confused pairs apart. You can also explain that PRINCE2 Agile governs projects using whichever of these approaches the delivery teams choose.

A.q: Which approach does the PRINCE2 Agile glossary describe as an iterative, timeboxed approach to product delivery?
A.why: The glossary describes Scrum as an iterative, timeboxed approach to product delivery.

whyNot.0: Kanban focuses on flow and WIP limits; it does not need timeboxed iterations.
whyNot.2: Lean Startup began as an approach for creating and managing start-ups.
whyNot.3: XP is known for engineering practices such as test-first programming, not timeboxed sprints as its core.

A.q: Which approach improves flow by visualizing work and controlling work in progress?
A.why: Kanban improves flow and provokes system improvement through visualization and controlling work in progress (Glossary).

whyNot.0: Scrum organizes work into timeboxed sprints with set accountabilities.
whyNot.3: XP centres on engineering practices such as test-first programming.

A.q: Which approach was originally used for creating and managing start-up companies?
A.why: The glossary says Lean Startup was originally an approach to creating and managing start-ups, now applied to any business.

whyNot.1: XP is known for engineering practices such as test-first programming.
whyNot.2: Scrum is a timeboxed framework for product delivery.
whyNot.3: Lean is about removing waste to maximize value; it did not start as a start-up approach.

B.q: Why does Kanban limit the number of work items in progress?
options: To fix the length of each sprint in advance
To set the priority order of the backlog
To estimate each story in story points
To expose bottlenecks in the process
B.why: Limiting the items in circulation in a pull system helps identify bottlenecks (Glossary).

whyNot.0: Kanban does not require sprints; fixing sprint length is a Scrum feature.
whyNot.1: Ordering the backlog is done by prioritization, not by WIP limits.
whyNot.2: Story points are an estimation technique, unrelated to WIP limits.

B.q: What is the main focus of Lean?
B.why: Lean focuses on delivering value with less waste, continually improving the flow of work.

whyNot.1: Timeboxed sprints with set accountabilities describe Scrum.
whyNot.2: Testing business ideas quickly describes Lean Startup.
whyNot.3: Test-first programming comes from eXtreme Programming.

B.q: Which approach is built around a build-measure-learn loop?
B.why: Lean Startup builds a minimum viable product, measures the response and learns, then decides to pivot or persevere.

whyNot.0: XP centres on engineering practices such as test-first programming, not a build-measure-learn loop.
whyNot.1: Scrum works in sprints with planning, review and retrospective.
whyNot.3: Lean is about removing waste; build-measure-learn is the Lean Startup loop.

C.q:
Which two statements are correct?
1. Scrum delivers work in timeboxed sprints.
2. Kanban requires sprints of a fixed length.
3. Kanban is a pull system that limits work in progress.
4. Lean Startup is a governance method for large projects.
C.why: Scrum is iterative and timeboxed (1), and Kanban is a pull system that limits work in progress (3).

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is wrong: Kanban does not need sprints or fixed iterations.
whyNot.2: Both are wrong: Kanban needs no sprints, and Lean Startup is not a governance method.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is wrong: Lean Startup is about delivering products to customers quickly through experiments.

C.q: A support team handles a continual stream of requests of varied size, has no fixed iteration cadence and wants to see where work gets stuck. Which approach fits best, and why?
options: Kanban, because it manages flow by limiting WIP
Scrum, because it manages flow by limiting WIP
Lean Startup, because it uses one-month sprints
Kanban, because it needs one-month sprints
C.why: Kanban suits continual, varied work: it visualizes flow and limits WIP to expose bottlenecks, without requiring iterations.

whyNot.1: Scrum is built on timeboxed sprints; flow with WIP limits is Kanban's defining feature.
whyNot.2: Lean Startup tests ideas with build-measure-learn; it is not sprint-based.
whyNot.3: Kanban is right, but it does not need sprints.

C.q: How does PRINCE2 Agile relate to approaches such as Scrum and Kanban?
options: It replaces them with its own delivery framework
It works with Scrum but excludes Kanban
It requires Lean Startup on every project
It adds governance around whichever is used
C.why: PRINCE2 Agile covers project direction and management, keeping governance and control, while delivery teams use the agile approach that suits them (3.1).

whyNot.0: PRINCE2 Agile does not replace delivery frameworks; it combines them with project management.
whyNot.1: Kanban is used within PRINCE2 Agile; the book even refers to Kanban cycles.
whyNot.2: No particular agile approach is mandatory.

reteach.title: Four kitchens
reteach.question: How would four different kitchens show the four approaches?

blocks.body: A Scrum kitchen plans a menu for a fixed two-week season, cooks it, then reviews it with diners. A Kanban kitchen takes orders as they come, with a limit on dishes on the pass at once, so a backlog at one station shows the bottleneck. A Lean kitchen keeps cutting waste from every step. A Lean Startup kitchen tries a new dish on a few tables, measures the reaction, and decides whether to keep it or change course.

blocks.text: Lean and Lean Startup are different: Lean removes waste; Lean Startup runs build-measure-learn experiments.

explain.body: An iterative, timeboxed approach to product delivery. Sprints last one month or less, with planning, a daily Scrum, a review and a retrospective. Accountabilities: product owner, Scrum master and developers.

test.q: Which feature is most characteristic of Scrum?
options: Work pulled in when capacity frees up
Timeboxed sprints of a month or less
Waste removal across the value stream
test.why: Scrum is an iterative, timeboxed approach; its sprints last one month or less.

whyNot.0: Pulling work when capacity frees up describes Kanban.
whyNot.1: Build-measure-learn is the Lean Startup loop.
whyNot.3: Removing waste is the focus of Lean.

explain.body: Visualize the work, limit work in progress and pull work in when there is capacity. Limits expose bottlenecks. No sprints are required.

options: Work is planned in fixed-length sprints
A manager assigns each task to a person
Customers pay before any work starts
Work is taken on when there is capacity
test.why: In a pull system, new work is pulled in only when capacity frees up, which Kanban enforces with WIP limits.

whyNot.0: Fixed sprints are a Scrum feature, not what makes Kanban a pull system.
whyNot.1: Assigning tasks from above is a push approach.
whyNot.2: Payment terms have nothing to do with a pull system.

explain.body: Start from what the customer values and remove whatever does not add to it. Keep improving the flow of work so value reaches customers with less waste.

test.q: A team maps every step of its process and removes those that add no value for the customer. Which approach is this most like?
test.why: Removing steps that add no customer value is the core idea of Lean.

whyNot.1: Scrum organizes work into sprints; it is not defined by waste removal.
whyNot.2: Lean Startup tests new business ideas with an MVP.
whyNot.3: XP focuses on engineering practices such as test-first programming.

explain.body: Originally for creating and managing start-ups, now used by any business to deliver products to customers quickly. Build a minimum viable product, measure the response, learn, then pivot or persevere.

test.q: After measuring how customers respond to a minimum viable product, a Lean Startup team decides whether to...
test.why: In Lean Startup, what the team learns from measuring leads to a decision to pivot or persevere.

whyNot.0: Limiting WIP is a Kanban practice.
whyNot.2: Starting the next sprint is a Scrum rhythm, not the Lean Startup decision.
whyNot.3: Removing waste is the focus of Lean.
